title: Private Deployments: VPC & On‑Prem Reference Guide — Deployment, Packaging, Day‑2 Ops, Upgrades & Rollbacks, Customer Requirements Library
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose: This page consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical guidance for private deployments (VPC-hosted and on‑prem), covering reference architectures, packaging and installation artifacts, day‑2 operational procedures, upgrade and rollback playbooks, and a customer requirements library. Intended for solutions engineers, SREs, and customer infra teams responsible for production private deployments.

Scope: VPC-based private control plane deployments, air‑gapped on‑prem installations (appliance or Kubernetes), packaging and distribution artifacts, day‑2 runbooks, upgrade/rollback procedures, and tenant/customer requirements checklist.

Sections: 1) Quick summary and decision table 2) Reference architectures 3) On‑prem packaging and distribution 4) VPC / Networking and security requirements 5) Day‑2 ops and monitoring 6) Upgrade and rollback procedures 7) Customer requirements library (checklist & templates) 8) Ownership, SLAs & escalation paths 9) Appendix: CLI/Helm/Terraform examples and configuration table

1) Quick summary and decision table

- Supported deployment modes: VPC (customer VPC with Redwood-managed control plane), Private control plane in customer VPC, Air‑gapped on‑prem (appliance or K8s package).
- Recommended first option for new customers: VPC private control plane (fastest onboarding, minimal packaging differences). On‑prem recommended when regulation or network isolation prohibits external control plane traffic.

Decision table (short):
Requirement | Recommended mode | Notes
---|---:|---
3rd‑party internet access allowed | VPC private control plane | Avoids air‑gap packaging complexity
Air‑gapped / HSM required | On‑prem appliance or K8s air‑gapped | Provide offline licenses & media
Large GPU footprint (customer colocation) | On‑prem | Local GPU drivers/kernels required

2) Reference architectures

2.1 VPC private control plane (typical customer-managed VPC)
- Components: customer VPC (subnets: control, worker, management), NAT/egress, private link / VPC peering for control plane, bastion/jump host, customer KMS/HSM endpoints, private registry for images (optional).
- Services and ownership:
  - Redwood control plane (SaaS) — Redwood (hosted) — optional private link endpoints.
  - Runtime workers (customer VPC) — customer manages instance types and autoscaling groups or k8s node pools.
  - Observability forwarding (Prometheus remote_write / OTLP) — customer endpoint owned by customer.
- High‑level diagram (textual):
  - Internet -> (optional) Private Link -> Redwood Control Plane -> customer VPC (API, autoscaling hooks) -> Worker subnets (intra VPC) -> GPUs / inference nodes

2.2 On‑prem Kubernetes reference (air‑gapped or connected)
- Components: On‑prem k8s cluster (prod namespace), storage (NFS/Ceph), private container registry (Harbor), KMS/HSM proxy, load balancer (MetalLB or F5), monitoring stack (Prometheus, Grafana, Loki), logging (Elastic or Splunk).
- Node sizing suggestion (starting): 3 control workers (2x management, 1x worker), GPU worker pool: start with 2 GPU nodes (A100 recommended) and scale per workload.

2.3 On‑prem appliance (single‑unit or HA pair)
- Components: prebuilt OS image with runtime, local registry, web UI for initial config, integrated metrics collector, USB/SSD recovery media for offline upgrades.

3) On‑prem packaging and distribution

3.1 Packaging options
- Helm chart bundle (recommended for k8s deployments): versioned chart tarball, value overrides template, CRDs separated.
- OCI image bundle (for air‑gapped): image tarballs + manifest + sha256 checksums. Delivered via SFTP or physical media per contract.
- Appliance ISO: signed OS image + provisioning scripts and post‑install config.

3.2 Delivery and integrity
- Signatures: All artifacts signed with Redwood release key. Verify with provided public key.
- Checksums: SHA256 for each artifact.
- Offline installation flow: 1) Transfer artifact.tar.gz -> verify checksum and signature -> import images to local registry -> apply CRDs and manifests -> bootstrap operator.

4) VPC / Networking and security requirements (minimal required list)

4.1 Network & firewall (customer responsibilities)
- Outbound / Inbound rules (example):
  - Allow outbound to Redwood control plane IPs: 3.34.12.0/24, 52.14.200.0/24 (replace with customer-specific range provided at contract).
  - Allow egress for container image pulls (AWS ECR / ghcr.io) or private registry endpoints.
  - Internal: worker -> control plane API port 8443 (TLS), key manager endpoints (443).
- Private Link: configure interface endpoints for control-plane endpoints when required.

4.2 Identity & secrets
- KMS/HSM integration: provide endpoint, credential rotation window, and allowed IAM principals.
- RBAC: OIDC / SAML integration recommended for operator access.
- Key trust model: Redwood signs image manifests; customer KMS used for model encryption at rest (optional).

4.3 Compliance & audit
- Audit logging: forward control plane and runtime audit logs to customer SIEM. Retention requirement template: 365 days or per contract.

5) Day‑2 operations (runbooks & monitoring)

5.1 Monitoring & alerting (recommended SLOs and thresholds)
- Platform SLOs (example):
  - API availability: 99.95% monthly
  - Median request latency (p50): < 150 ms for non‑batched requests
  - Error rate (5xx): < 0.5%
- Key alerts (examples):
  - Worker node GPU memory pressure > 85% for 5m -> severity P2
  - Queue depth (inference backlog) > 1000 requests for 10m -> P1
  - Model load failures > 3 in 10m -> P1
  - Control plane heartbeat missing for > 2m -> P1

5.2 Runbooks (day‑2 playbook summary)
- Routine tasks: certificate rotation (quarterly), KMS credential rotation (as scheduled), OS and security patching windows, node pool scaling, model artifact garbage collection.
- Incident triage steps (simplified):
  1. Identify scope (single pod, node, or cluster).
  2. Check control plane connectivity and API tokens.
  3. Inspect logs (operator, runtime, kubelet) and metrics (GPU utilization, queue depth).
  4. Mitigate (restart pods, cordon/evict node, autoscale additional workers).
  5. Escalate to Redwood support if control plane or runtime core library errors persist.

5.3 Backups and recovery
- Regular backups: PostgreSQL config DB snapshot (daily), model artifacts metadata (hourly incremental), Kubernetes resource manifests (after each change).
- Restore test: Quarterly DR test for configuration and metadata restore.

6) Upgrade and rollback procedures

6.1 Pre‑upgrade checklist
- Verify backups exist and are validated.
- Verify operator compatibility matrix for current k8s/node drivers (see Appendix table).
- Validate canary namespace and smoke tests (prompt set, small model run).
- Notify teams and schedule maintenance window if required per SLA.

6.2 Upgrade procedure (Kubernetes Helm flow)
1. Create new release tag and prepare chart values file: values-<release>.yaml.
2. Push images to private registry (or make available in customer registry).
3. Dry‑run helm upgrade in staging: helm upgrade --install --dry-run --namespace staging redwood-platform ./chart -f values-<release>.yaml.
4. Run automated smoke tests against staging.
5. Promote to canary in production (single node or single AZ): helm upgrade --namespace prod --set canary=true redwood-platform ./chart -f values-<release>.yaml.
6. Monitor canary for 30‑60 minutes: health endpoints, prometheus alerts, synthetic prompt latency.
7. If canary healthy, rollout to remaining nodes: helm upgrade --namespace prod redwood-platform ./chart -f values-<release>.yaml.
8. Post‑upgrade validation: run post‑upgrade smoke tests, verify model load success, check metrics.

6.3 Rollback procedure
- If a canary fails or production regressions detected, perform:
  1. helm rollback redwood-platform <previous-release> --namespace prod.
  2. If kernel/driver-level incompatibility suspected, cordon GPU nodes and switch to fallback instance type (see fallback policy below).
  3. Revert DNS or LB traffic split if using traffic routing.
  4. Create postmortem and tag as rollback event in release tracker.

6.4 Fallback policy and automated protections
- Automatic fallback to a known-good model variant or smaller batch config if latency or OOMs spike.
- Circuit breaker: if error rate > 2% for 5m, temporarily reduce concurrency and enable degraded mode (no‑cache, smaller batch).

7) Customer requirements library (checklist & templates)

7.1 Minimum customer deliverables before kickoff
- Completed network diagram (drawn to scale), CIDR allocations, and egress IPs.
- KMS endpoint + test credentials and owner contact.
- Container registry access or credentialed S3 for artifacts.
- List of approved instance types and GPU SKUs.
- Compliance constraints: data residency, retention, encryption requirements.

7.2 Onboarding checklist (to be completed by solutions engineer + customer)
- [ ] Network peering/private link configured and tested
- [ ] NAT/egress rules in place for image pulls
- [ ] KMS/HSM integration tested with sample encryption/decryption
- [ ] Monitoring endpoints (Prometheus/OTLP) reachable and credentials provided
- [ ] SIEM forwarding configured for audit logs
- [ ] SSH bastion + RBAC/OIDC access validated
- [ ] Backup targets and restore test scheduled

7.3 Templates included in attachments (deliverables)
- Network diagram template (draw.io)
- Example values.yaml (helm) for VPC and on‑prem
- Upgrade runbook template (Markdown)
- Customer acceptance test (CAT) prompt set and expected metrics

8) Ownership, SLAs & escalation paths

- Ownership matrix:
  - Networking and compute: Customer (with Redwood assistance during onboarding)
  - Control plane availability (hosted): Redwood (unless private control plane deployed in customer VPC per contract)
  - Runtime & model loading failures: Joint ownership — initial triage by customer SRE then Redwood runtime team if operator errors appear.
- Escalation: Follow the standard Redwood incident process — open support ticket -> escalate to on‑call runtime engineer -> involve product/security as required. Include contact SRE Pager and support SLAs in contract.

9) Appendix: CLI, Helm and Terraform examples & compatibility table

9.1 Example Helm values snippet (VPC deployment)
----
replicaCount: 3
runtime:
  enableGpuNodePool: true
  gpuInstanceType: p4d.24xlarge
controlPlane:
  endpoint: "https://redwood-control.example.internal"
  tls:
    caFile: "/etc/pki/ca.pem"
kms:
  provider: aws-kms
  endpoint: "https://kms.customer.internal"
----

9.2 Terraform quick example (VPC endpoint)
----
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "redwood_control" {
  vpc_id            = var.vpc_id
  service_name      = "com.amazonaws.vpce.redwood-control"
  subnet_ids        = var.subnet_ids
  security_group_ids = [var.endpoint_sg]
}
----

9.3 Compatibility & kernel matrix (excerpt)
Component | Minimum version | Notes
---|---:|---
Kubernetes | 1.24 | Use supported kubelets with runtime operator
NVIDIA drivers | 525.x | See runtime release notes for optimized kernels
CUDA | 11.8 | Required for A100 optimized execution

9.4 Example rollback metadata to record (required post‑rollback)
- Release tag rolled back
- Time window and impacted AZs
- Root cause hypothesis
- Actions taken and follow‑up tasks
